summary: Describes two ways a DNSSEC-validating resolver can tell a server which trust anchor keys it uses. That helps zone administrators watch the progress of key rollovers. An update to it exists as RFC 8553.

eli5.summary: When a school changes its secret handshake, the teacher wants to know which kids learned the new one. This is how kids can say which handshake they know.

questions: how to monitor dnssec key rollover
how does dnssec key tag signaling work
what is a _ta query in dns
how to monitor dnssec root key rollover
subtitle: How a DNSSEC validating resolver can tell a server which trust anchor keys it uses, so key rollovers can be watched.

tldr.problem: When a DNSSEC zone such as the root rolls over its keys, administrators have no way to see how many validating resolvers have picked up the new trust anchor.
tldr.mechanism: A validating resolver reports the Key Tags of its trust anchors in one of two optional ways: an edns-key-tag option (option code 14) on DNSKEY queries, or a separate NULL query whose name starts with _ta- followed by the hexadecimal Key Tags.
tldr.outcome: Authoritative servers can log the signals and judge when a rollover is safe to complete. The document was later updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 8145 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8553. Both signaling mechanisms are optional to implement and use.

sections.title: Why Signal Trust Anchor Knowledge
sections.content:
DNSSEC protects DNS data with digital signatures. A validating resolver checks them by building a chain of trust that starts at a trust anchor, a configured DNSKEY record or the hash of one. The root zone is the case the RFC cares about most: when its keys or algorithms roll over using RFC 5011, resolvers update their trust anchors automatically, and the zone operators cannot tell who has done so.

RFC 8145 gives resolvers two optional ways to tell a server which keys they would use to validate its answers. The data lets zone administrators gauge the deployment of new keys. The RFC is clear that it introduces no new process for rolling keys or updating trust anchors. It only signals the set of keys a client uses.
sections.eli5: When the teacher changes the secret handshake, she needs to know when enough kids have learned it. Without a way to ask, she is guessing.

sections.title: Key Tags and Trust Anchors
sections.content:
A Key Tag is a 16-bit number computed from the RDATA of a DNSKEY record, using a formula not unlike a ones-complement checksum. It exists so software can quickly pick the right key when several are candidates. RRSIG records and DS records both carry a Key Tag field that points at the DNSKEY involved.

Because the Key Tag is short and already public, it makes a compact way to say which key a resolver is using. A resolver learns the Key Tags of a zone's key signing keys from the zone's DS records in the parent or from a trust anchor. DNSSEC does not require Key Tags to be unique, so the RFC warns that during a rollover an old and a new key could, with small probability, share the same tag. Zone operators relying on the edns-key-tag mechanism SHOULD make sure new keys have unique Key Tags.
sections.eli5: A Key Tag is like a short number on a key ring tag, so you can find the right key without trying all of them.

sections.title: The edns-key-tag Option
sections.content:
The first method puts the Key Tags into an EDNS option in the OPT record of a DNS query. The option code is 14. OPTION-LENGTH is 2 times the number of Key Tags, followed by one or more 16-bit KEY-TAG values.

A validating resolver sets the option when it sends a DNSKEY query, and SHOULD also set the DO bit. The tags represent the keys it expects to validate the response with. A client SHOULD include the option for a DNSKEY query for a zone with a trust anchor, and MAY include it for other zones, using tags learned from DS records. It MUST NOT include the option on non-DNSKEY queries, and MUST NOT include tags for keys not learned from a trust anchor or DS record. Non-validating stub resolvers MUST NOT include the option at all.

Recursive resolvers have extra rules. If a client's Key Tag list differs from the resolver's own, the resolver SHOULD forward both lists, each in a separate instance of the option. The RFC's example is a resolver list of (19036, 12345) and a client list of (19036, 34567). A recursive resolver MAY combine tags from several clients, and is RECOMMENDED to limit how many it includes. A non-validating recursive resolver SHOULD copy the option it received. Responders MUST NOT include the option in any response, and a client that sees it in a response MUST ignore it.
sections.eli5: The resolver tucks a little note onto its question saying which keys it knows. The server never writes a note back.

sections.title: The Key Tag Query
sections.content:
The second method sends a separate query. A Key Tag query is a standard DNS query of type NULL and class IN. The first label of the name is _ta- followed by a sorted, hyphen-separated list of hexadecimal Key Tags, with the trust anchor's zone name appended. Each value MUST be zero-padded to four hexadecimal digits, so decimal 999 becomes 03e7, and multiple tags MUST be sorted from smallest to largest.

A validating resolver SHOULD send a Key Tag query whenever it sends a DNSKEY query for a trust anchor zone, and SHOULD NOT do so for non-trust-anchor zones. A non-validating resolver MUST NOT send them. Resolvers with caches SHOULD cache the answer like any other.

Authoritative servers MAY log the queries. The server needs no special logic; the response code depends on whether the name is in the zone or covered by wildcards. Zone operators may add Key Tag records, with chosen TTLs, to influence how often clients ask. This also matters for aggressive NSEC/NSEC3 negative caching: if answers are NXDOMAIN, resolvers that implement it will send fewer Key Tag queries than those that do not. During a rollover from Key Tag 1111 to 2222 (hex), the RFC suggests publishing _ta-1111, _ta-2222 and _ta-1111-2222 as empty NULL records.
sections.eli5: Instead of a note on the question, the resolver asks a made-up question whose words spell out the keys it knows. The server just reads the question.

sections.title: Why There Are Two Methods
sections.content:
The work started with only the EDNS option, modeled on RFC 6975 (DNSSEC algorithm signaling). DNSOP working group participants suggested using the query name instead, because forwarding makes EDNS awkward. EDNS(0) is hop-by-hop, so unknown option codes are not forwarded by default, middleboxes might block queries with unknown options, and a recursive resolver might need to remember tags from its clients.

The EDNS option still has an advantage: it can show that a stub client has a different Key Tag list from its forwarder. The authors judged this not enough to drop the QNAME approach. The QNAME approach has downsides too: it needs a separate query, it can be affected by aggressive negative caching, and it cannot be used when adding the prefix would push a name beyond 255 octets. For this reason the RFC recommends Key Tag queries only for trust anchors, while EDNS-based tags can go on any DNSKEY query.
sections.eli5: The authors first wrote notes on the question, then found notes can get lost on the way, so they added the made-up-question trick too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An eavesdropper or server could infer which validator a client uses from its Key Tag list. That might let an attacker find validators with old, possibly broken keys, or narrow down implementations that have a known vulnerability.

Consumers of the collected data are also warned that Key Tag values may be made up. An attacker with enough resources could send many queries listing only old Key Tags to delay the completion of a key rollover.
sections.eli5: Someone listening could learn which handshake you know, and someone could lie about it to keep the teacher from ever switching.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Key Tag values are not considered private, but an eavesdropper might use them to fingerprint particular validating clients, especially if the validator has trust anchors for zones beyond the root. A resolver need not send tags on every query; it MAY send them for a subset, such as every 25th time or with a probability such as 5%. Implementations MAY be configured to send tags only for certain zones.

Since the main goal is measuring root zone rollovers, implementations are RECOMMENDED to at least include the edns-key-tag option for root zone DNSKEY queries.
sections.eli5: You do not have to tell the teacher every time. You can mention it now and then, or only for certain classes.

fields.name: OPTION-CODE
fields.desc: The EDNS0 option code assigned to edns-key-tag.

fields.name: OPTION-LENGTH
fields.desc: 2 x the number of key-tag values present.

fields.name: KEY-TAG
fields.desc: One or more 16-bit Key Tag values; the list may continue.
